list.listitem: Pathologic discharge and discharge associated with a palpable mass or mammographic abnormality is more likely to be malignant, as is discharge in postmenopausal women, transgender women, or in men. B

A careful breast examination, mammogram, and ultrasound are used for diagnosis in women older than 30 years, transgender women, and men. Consider an ultrasound for imaging in women younger than 30 years. B
Duct excision is recommended for both diagnosis and treatment in patients with a pathologic discharge. B
Benign nipple discharge usually resolves spontaneously within 1 to 6 months, but may last years. B

background.definition: Discharge, or release of fluid, from the ducts in the nipple is most often a benign finding; discharge that is spontaneous, persistent, unilateral, or from a single duct is of greater concern.

list.listitem: Approximately 2% to 5% of women seeking care in breast clinics complain of nipple discharge.

Reported prevalence of nipple discharge was 0.3% to 0.4% at 1,198,410 breast cancer screening visits among women aged 50 to 69 years in Finland (2006–2010). This represented a small portion of the 24.9% who reported at least one breast symptom, including presence of a scar or mole, nipple retraction, or breast lump (the latter reported by 1.3%-1.5%).
Nipple discharge is the third most common breast complaint, after breast pain and breast mass.

One percent to five percent of breast cancers present as nipple discharge. Risk factors for malignancy include discharge in postmenopausal women; any discharge associated with a palpable mass; unilateral, spontaneous, or persistent discharge; bloody or serous discharge; and nipple discharge in a male.
In a prospective UK study of 228 new patients presenting with unilateral nipple discharge to one of 5 breast units, incidence of malignancy was 4.4%.

In the paper on breast cancer screening from Finland noted above, breast cancer was identified in 6,009 women (0.5%), and the presence of nipple discharge increased the risk of breast cancer by more than twofold (OR 2.14; 95% CI, 1.58-2.89) compared to women who reported no breast-related symptoms. Of the 3965 women reporting nipple discharge, breast cancer was diagnosed in 43 (1.08%).
Ten to fifty percent of patients with benign breast disease have a nipple discharge, especially with papillomas.

Galactorrhea is a milky discharge that may be physiologic or may signal an endocrine disorder, medication side effect (), or occur as a result of chest wall trauma, but does not signal significant breast pathology.
Infections in the breast, including mastitis and abscess.
Mammary duct ectasia and fibrocystic disease.
Intraductal papilloma and papillomatosis.

Malignancy, usually ductal carcinoma or papillary carcinoma, is an uncommon but concerning cause of nipple discharge. In one case series of patients with bloody nipple discharge, 24 of 89 examined histologically were neuroendocrine carcinomas which made up nearly half (24/55) of the mammary cancers found because of discharge.

Galactorrhea or milk production is regulated mainly by prolactin production from the anterior pituitary and dopamine inhibition from the hypothalamus. Any situation that increases the prolactin level or inhibits dopamine regulation can result in an inappropriate production of milk.
All other nipple discharge is caused by ductal lesions, benign or malignant.
Ductal ectasia, hyperplasia, and fibrocystic changes in the breast cause dilation of the ducts with resulting inflammation and fibrosis.

Intraductal papillomas and carcinomas may cause a bloody nipple discharge. Investigators found an association between human papilloma virus (HPV) and ductal papilloma; HPV was present in 8 of 27 (29.6%) specimens obtained through ductoscopic papilloma extraction.

Asking about and trying to elicit nipple discharge is part of the clinical breast examination (CBE). While recommended by the American Cancer Society, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (2016) found insufficient evidence regarding value of the CBE. B
Excessive nipple manipulation may cause nipple discharge and should be avoided if discharge develops. C
Pathologic discharge is more likely to be malignant and require further evaluation. B
Discharge in association with a palpable mass or mammographic abnormality is more likely to be malignant, as is discharge in postmenopausal women, transgender women, or in men. B
If galactorrhea is present, order a prolactin level, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), and a pregnancy test. B

A careful breast examination, mammogram and ultrasound are essential for diagnosis in women with nipple discharge who are older than 30 years. Consider an ultrasound in women younger than 30 years. B The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG, 2016) recommend ultrasound in women with spontaneous, unilateral, uni-ductal nipple discharge that is clear, serous, or bloody. C
Postmenopausal women and men of any age with pathologic nipple discharge should undergo duct excision because of the increased risk for cancer. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Single duct, unilateral, possible abnormal mammogram or ultrasound
Single duct, unilateral, abnormal imaging, bloody discharge, possible mass

list.listitem: The history should include the age of the patient, a menstrual and pregnancy history, and a description of the nipple discharge to include color and duration, single or multiple ducts, unilateral or bilateral discharge, and whether it is spontaneous or provoked.
A medication history is important since many medications can affect dopamine and prolactin levels causing galactorrhea (see ).
It is important to ask about any palpable masses in the breast tissue.
Other related symptoms such as vision changes, headache, cold intolerance, and fatigue may be related to pituitary or thyroid abnormalities causing nipple discharge.

The physical examination should include a thorough breast examination including the nipple, skin of the breast, and axilla. It is important to exclude the presence of a mass in the breast. Attempt to elicit discharge from the nipple to determine which duct or ducts are involved. Good lighting and a magnifying glass are helpful. Examination of the thyroid gland (hypothyroidism/goiter) and visual fields should also be included if the discharge is milky (galactorrhea).
Bilateral, multiductal, provoked discharges that are white, yellow, green, or brown are more likely to represent a benign condition.

Unilateral, single duct, spontaneous discharges that are clear, serous, bloody, or serosanguineous are more indicative of pathology, as is discharge associated with a mass, in older women, and in men. In a meta-analysis of 8 studies with 1,632 patients, the 25% in the bloody nipple discharge group had a higher breast cancer risk than patients with non-bloody nipple discharge (OR 2.27; 95% CI, 1.32-3.89). They also had a higher breast cancer risk than those in the clear/serous discharge group (OR 2.49; 95% CI, 1.25-4.93).
The likelihood of malignancy in a woman with pathologic discharge referred for evaluation ranges from 9% to 20% in different studies.

The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2022 update) noted that imaging is not indicated for women with physiologic nipple discharge. For pathologic nipple discharge, they recommend the following: For women age 40 years or older, mammography or digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) is recommended as initial examination with ultrasound usually added as a complementary examination. For women age 30 to 39 years, ACR recommends either mammogram or ultrasound as the initial examination. For women age 30 years or younger, ACR recommends ultrasound as the initial examination, with mammography/DBT added if ultrasound shows suspicious findings or if the patient is predisposed to developing breast cancer. For men age 25 or older, mammography/DBT should be performed initially, with ultrasound added as indicated. Adult transfeminine patient, mammography/DBT should be performed initially, with ultrasound added as indicated. Transgender women who are taking gender affirming hormones, even for short durations, are at increased risk for breast cancer.
ACOG recommends ultrasound in women with spontaneous, unilateral, uni-ductal nipple discharge that is clear, serous, or bloody.

Mammography in women older than 30 years is standard practice; however, negative results do not reliably exclude malignancy. Ultrasound, may be used to further identify a lesion or diagnose benign ductal disease, and may be a useful adjunct to mammography. It is considered first line for women younger than 30 years, although the LR+ is low for cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ.

In the UK study of 228 new patients with unilateral discharge, the positive predictive value for detecting malignancy for an abnormality found on ultrasonography was 65.2% and for mammography was 53.5%.

Ductography (contrast material injected into the duct, followed by mammogram) may help localize a lesion, but may miss up to 20% of ductal lesions, including cases where there are multiple lesions or lesions in the breast periphery. Ductography cannot distinguish between benign and malignant lesions (LR+ 1.5).

Ductoscopy (an endoscopic examination) provides a way to directly visualize an intraductal lesion and aspirate or biopsy that lesion. The appearance of a lesion may provide a clue to diagnosis. For example, amorphous lesions are more likely to be malignant. However, ductoscopy does not reliably distinguish between benign and malignant lesions and is still being investigated. It is used more often to identify the symptomatic duct for more selective surgical excision.

Ductoscopy may reduce the need for surgical excision in patients with pathologic nipple discharge. In one case series of 215 consecutive patients with pathologic nipple discharge, the procedure was successful in 151 and an underlying cause for PND was visualized in 102, of whom 82 patients were treated without surgery. Sixty of the 215 patients eventually underwent surgery and a malignancy was found in 7 (5 of them classified as suspicious at ductoscopy). No serious side effects were reported.

In a second case series, none of the 85 patients with a successful and negative ductoscopy developed malignancy at a median follow-up of 2 years. Of the 125 with an identified intraductal mass of whom 82 underwent microdochectomy, 15 malignancies were diagnosed.

In one study, a positive ductoscopy showing a papillomatous lesion was a better predictor of the presence of intraductal neoplasia than meeting all 3-criteria (spontaneous, single duct, bloody or serous) for pathologic nipple discharge. The area under curve was 0.9 (95% CI, 0.8-0.98) compared with 0.7 (95% CI, 0.6-0.8), respectively. None of the 21 women with negative ductoscopy who were followed without duct excision developed signs of malignancy or required biopsy during a 48-month follow-up period.

Breast MRI with contrast may help distinguish between benign and malignant lesions; recent studies have demonstrated fairly good sensitivity, although lower specificity, for diagnosis of ductal carcinoma in situ. Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies with 921 patients with pathologic nipple discharge found a pooled sensitivity and specificity for cancer detection with MRI of 92% (95% CI, 74%-98%) and 97% (95% CI, 80%-100%), respectively. MRI demonstrated higher or similar sensitivity and specificity in detecting cancer compared to ductoscopy, and higher values than galactography, and would be a reasonable next step in evaluating pathologic nipple discharge if mammogram and ultrasound are negative, and is more comfortable for the patient; however, is not indicated as initial imaging.

Authors of a review of use of MRI for pathologic nipple discharge note that when initial imaging with mammogram and ultrasound are negative, MRI is able to identify the cause of nipple discharge in 56% to 61% of cases. Conditions that are well visualized using this imaging method include papillomas and nipple adenomas, ductal ectasia, infectious etiologies such as abscess, and fistulas, Paget's disease, ductal carcinoma in-situ (DCIS), and invasive carcinoma.

Among 320 consecutive patients presenting with nipple discharge in a single institution, of whom 12.5% had confirmed breast malignancy, the combination of digital mammography and ultrasound had a 93% sensitivity and a 98% NPV for malignancy, while contrast enhanced MRI (CE-MRI) had a 100% sensitivity and a 100% NPV for malignancy.

In one case series of 82 women with pathological nipple discharge undergoing diagnostic microdochectomy who had no malignancy identified on pre-operative mammography or ultrasound, malignancy was identified in 14 patients (17%). Sensitivity of preoperative MRI in detecting an occult malignancy was 85.7% and the specificity was 98.5%. The positive predictive value (PPV) was 92.3% and the negative predictive value (NPV) was 97.1%. In a retrospective series of 105 women with nipple discharge and a negative or inconclusive mammogram who underwent surgical excision or at least 2-year imaging follow-up, 27 had a positive MRI of whom 3 were diagnosed with malignancy for a much lower PPV of 11.1% (3/27). Three women who had a negative MRI were diagnosed with grade 1 ductal carcinoma in-situ for a NPV of 96.2% (75/78).

Cytology of the nipple discharge may complement the evaluation of nipple discharge as a specific but not sensitive test. It is only clearly useful if abnormal and is not routinely recommended, but may be used in combination with abnormal breast imaging. Guaiac testing of the discharge can be done to confirm the presence of blood.

Surgical duct excision should be offered to all women with unilateral, bloody, or otherwise suspicious nipple discharge, especially if persistent, to exclude malignancy. Duct excision may be therapeutic, as well. A core biopsy should be undertaken if a mass is identified.
If galactorrhea is present, exclude pregnancy then check serum prolactin and TSH. Consider an MRI of the pituitary gland if the prolactin is abnormally high.

See for a suggested approach to evaluation. Classify discharge as benign (white, yellow, green, or brown; nonspontaneous; bilateral; multiple ducts) versus pathologic (clear, serous, bloody, or serosanguineous; unilateral; single duct; spontaneous; associated with breast mass).
For galactorrhea, exclude pregnancy and check serum prolactin and TSH. Consider an MRI of the pituitary gland if the prolactin is abnormally high.

A surgical procedure (core or excisional biopsy) is recommended for women with a pathologic discharge and any discharge in a man. If there is a mass present or the mammogram results are BI-RADs (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data Systems) score 4 or 5 (suspicious or highly suspicious), biopsy is necessary.
Galactorrhea may be treated with a dopamine agonist if symptoms are bothersome, fertility is desired, and for preservation of bone density. B
Major duct excision is the definitive test for diagnosis and treatment of nipple discharge. B
Benign nipple discharge of ductal origin can be treated with single duct excision if symptoms do not resolve spontaneously. C
Physiologic nipple discharge may be followed clinically without extensive work-up. C

If galactorrhea is present, a dopamine agonist such as bromocriptine 2.5 to 10 mg daily (Parlodel) or cabergoline 0.25 to 2 mg weekly (Dostinex) may be used if symptoms are bothersome, fertility is desired, to help with bone density preservation, or if a pituitary adenoma is enlarging.
Galactorrhea: avoid medications that can cause galactorrhea if possible ().

Surgery is rarely needed in low-risk cases of nipple discharge. If a nipple discharge is bilateral, multiductal and no mass is present, the patient may be followed clinically. Surgery is considered if the discharge persists for more than a year or becomes too irritating to the patient.
If there is a mass present, biopsy is necessary.

If the discharge is more consistent with a pathologic cause—unilateral, single duct, spontaneous, serosanguineous—major duct excision is the procedure of choice unless breast feeding in the future is desired.

Ultrasound-guided wire localization with targeted tissue excision may be a good option in women with focal duct dilatation associated with nipple discharge. In a case series of 56 such patients of whom 44 (78.5%) had bloody nipple discharge, preoperative ultrasound-guided wire localization of the site was successfully performed in all cases. Findings were papilloma alone in 40 cases (71.4%), papilloma + ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in six patients (10.7%), papilloma + invasive ductal carcinoma in six patients (10.7%), DCIS in two patients (3.6%) and duct ectasia in two patients (3.6%).

Based on a case series, potential candidates for observation despite a pathological nipple discharge are those with normal exams and normal breast imaging. In this case series, among the 46 patients who fit this description, only one malignancy was identified in a 79-year-old patient with a personal history of breast cancer. None of the 23 patients who opted for observation over duct excision were diagnosed with cancer at a mean follow-up of 3.3 years.
If breast feeding is desired, microdochectomy removes less tissue and may be an option.
In the case of galactorrhea caused by a pituitary macroadenoma, transsphenoidal resection may be performed if neurologic symptoms are developing or symptoms are not controlled with medications.

Patients with nipple discharge that has benign features may be followed conservatively. These patients are instructed to avoid breast manipulation and report any spontaneous discharge or changes in symptoms.
Refer to a surgeon if a mass is present or tissue diagnosis is indicated.
Refer to a surgeon or breast center if you are not comfortable completing the evaluation of nipple discharge to exclude malignancy.
Benign nipple discharge usually resolves spontaneously within 1 to 6 months, but may last years. B
There is not an increased risk of breast carcinoma if the discharge is of a benign nature and there is no mass detected. Regular periodic follow-up is recommended until the discharge resolves. B
Follow-up examinations and mammograms should be performed every 6 months for 2 years after onset of a benign-appearing nipple discharge. B
Nipple discharge in postmenopausal women has a higher association with an underlying cancer and a more aggressive approach is indicated.
A milky discharge from the nipple is normal in pregnancy; however, a non-lactational discharge needs to be evaluated further, similar to evaluation in a nonpregnant woman.
Galactorrhea can persist up to 1 year postpartum or post breastfeeding.

A bloody nipple discharge due to endothelial proliferation in the second and third trimesters is physiologic and reassurance may be given as long as this is the sole complaint. If a bloody discharge persists beyond 2 months after delivery, it must be investigated.
Mammogram and ultrasound are more difficult to interpret in pregnancy because of increased blood supply and proliferative changes in the breast associated with pregnancy.
Tissue biopsy is recommended if there is a palpable mass.
A milky nipple discharge in newborns and early adolescents is common and due to hormonal changes in the first few months of life and during puberty.

Bilateral bloody nipple discharge in infants and children is rare and can be followed closely in the absence of a mass. This is usually due to mammary duct ectasia and is self-limiting. Serial follow-up ultrasounds can be used; findings include dilated ducts and tubular anechoic lesions with or without echogenic debris.
Breast malignancy is extremely rare; however, if a biopsy or surgery is warranted for a mass or a persistent, unilateral discharge, care must be taken to minimize breast deformity.

Mammogram (ultrasound if age <30); likely duct ectasia; monitor if results are negative; consider referral if bothersome.
Mammogram plus needle biopsy or referral; see chapter on breast lump.
Single duct, bloody, clear or serous?
Ultrasound, mammogram if age >30, referral for duct excision if BI-RADs 1-3, tissue biopsy if BI-RADS 4-5.
Ultrasound, mammogram if age >30; consider referral for ductography or ductoscopy, tissue biopsy if BI-RADS 4-5.
Yellow-green or dark green and nonbloody discharge?
Serous or bloody discharge or mass present?
Likely ductal ectasia or fibrocystic breast; monitor, order mammogram if over age 40; consider mammogram if over age 30 or ultrasound if under age 30 years.
Check serum prolactin and TSH; consider a pituitary MRI if prolactin is high.
Monitor; consider serum prolactin or TSH if persistent.
